**Aswad** are a British [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae "Reggae") group, noted for adding strong [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B") and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") influences to the reggae sound.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-1) They have been performing since the mid-1970s, and have released 21 albums. Their [UK hit singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") include the [number one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chart-topper "Chart-topper") "[Don't Turn Around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Turn_Around "Don't Turn Around")" (1988) and "[Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shine_(Aswad_song) "Shine (Aswad song)")" (1994). "Aswad" is [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language") for "[black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black "Black")". They are three-time [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nominees.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aswad&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The members of Aswad are UK descendants of immigrants from the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). They attended John Kelly/[Holland Park School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Park_School "Holland Park School"). Aswad was formed in 1975 in the [Ladbroke Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladbroke_Grove "Ladbroke Grove") area of [West London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_London "West London").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-3)

The original members of Aswad were guitarist/vocalist [Brinsley "Chaka B" Forde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brinsley_Forde "Brinsley Forde"), drummer/vocalist [Angus "Drummie Zeb" Gaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummie_Zeb "Drummie Zeb"), lead guitarist/vocalist Donald "Dee" Griffiths, bassist George "Ras" Oban, and keyboardist Courtney "Khaki" Hemmings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) Aswad were the backing band of [Burning Spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_Spear "Burning Spear")'s 1977 _[Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_(Burning\_Spear\_album) "Live (Burning Spear album)")_ album, recorded at the [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre") in London. Other contributors included [Vin Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vin_Gordon "Vin Gordon"), and [Karl Pitterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Pitterson "Karl Pitterson").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Larkin-5)

Initially, the band produced music in the [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") vein, with members contributing songs individually and with Forde acting as the band's principal songwriter. The band's dynamic soon began to change however. Shortly after the release of their self-titled debut album in 1976, Hemmings left and was replaced by Tony "Gad" Robinson (the only time in the band's history where a departing member would be officially replaced by an incoming musician). The band then released their second studio effort, _Hulet_, in 1978, before George Oban ( who later played with [Burning Spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_Spear "Burning Spear") and [African Headcharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Headcharge "African Headcharge") ) departed the band in 1979, with Robinson taking over the position of bassist as well as continuing his role as keyboardist. The following year saw Griffiths depart, leaving Forde as the band's sole guitarist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) During this early period in the band's history they were distinctly different from Jamaican reggae acts, in that they wrote songs that dealt with the issues surrounding the experiences of black youths growing-up in the UK;[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) such as "Three Babylon" and "It's Not Our Wish","Natural Progression", "Ghetto in the Sky". and the powerful [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")-influenced [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental "Instrumental") "Warrior Charge", which is still much played by [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") sound systems worldwide. The band continued making [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") and dub music, and in 1985, released _[Jah Shaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jah\_Shaka "Jah Shaka") Meets Aswad in [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis\_Ababa "Addis Ababa") Studio._

Once the band's line-up had stabilised into the trio of Forde, Gaye, and Robinson, Aswad followed a more commercial reggae style, gaining a wider audience with the _New Chapter_ album (1981). They then followed this with the Michael Reuben Campbell-produced _[A New Chapter of Dub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_New\_Chapter\_of\_Dub "A New Chapter of Dub")_ LP which was a dub of the entire _New Chapter_ album. Clifton "Bigga" Morrison of [Prince Far I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Far_I "Prince Far I")'s band, The Arabs, played bass on some of the tracks. _Not Satisfied_ was a London roots-reggae album released in 1982. In August 1983, Aswad played live at [Meanwhile Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meanwhile_Gardens "Meanwhile Gardens") on the Sunday of the [Notting Hill Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Carnival "Notting Hill Carnival"); the resulting live album _Live and Direct_ is a faithful record of that event, where they played a live dub set. "Love Fire" gained wide recognition when it was used as the [backing rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riddim "Riddim") for [Dennis Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Brown "Dennis Brown")'s "Promised Land".

Among Aswad's catalogue of [hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_single "Hit single") is "[Don't Turn Around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Turn_Around "Don't Turn Around")", a UK No. 1 hit in 1988,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-6) originally recorded by [Tina Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Turner "Tina Turner") as a [B-side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-side_and_B-side "A-side and B-side") to her "[Typical Male](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typical_Male "Typical Male")" single. They followed this up with UK No. 11 hit "Give a Little Love",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-6) and a reggae-flavoured rendition of "[Best of My Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_of_My_Love_(Eagles_song) "Best of My Love (Eagles song)")", first popularised and written by [The Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eagles "The Eagles"). In 1989, they contributed the single "Set Them Free" to the [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace")_Rainbow Warriors_ album. In the same year, they performed together with [Cliff Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliff_Richard "Cliff Richard") the song "Share a Dream", recorded the previous year, at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium") as part of The Event (16 and 17 June 1989). Their next single, "[Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shine_(Aswad_song) "Shine (Aswad song)")", was released in 1994 and was a big hit in much of Europe. Another track was the upbeat 1998 remake of [The Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Police "The Police")'s "[Invisible Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invisible_Sun "Invisible Sun")", performed with [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)").

The band also hold the distinction of having played with each one of the ex-[Wailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wailers_(1963-1974_band) "The Wailers (1963-1974 band)").

The band has toured extensively, playing in diverse locations from London's [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") and [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay")'s [Reggae Sunsplash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae_Sunsplash "Reggae Sunsplash"), to gigs in West Africa, [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") and Japan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-7)

Aswad underwent their first line-up change in sixteen years in 1996, when Forde departed the band for spiritual reasons, leaving Gaye as the only founding member. Once again, the remaining members opted not to seek to recruit a replacement musician, and thus Aswad became a duo of Gaye and Robinson. With the exception of a brief reunion with Forde in 2009 for the Island record label's 50th-anniversary celebrations,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-8) the band's line-up remained the same until Angus Gaye’s death on 2 September 2022, aged 62.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-9)

Aswad released their final studio album to date in 2009, with _City Lock_. They released the singles "What Is Love?" and "Do That Thing" in the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-10)

Aswad toured the UK in Spring 2025, including playing at the [Lambeth Country Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Country_Show "Lambeth Country Show"), at [Butlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butlins "Butlins") resorts, [Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth "Bournemouth")'s Reggae Weekender, and with [Ali Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Campbell "Ali Campbell")'s [UB40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UB40 "UB40") at [Colchester Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester_Castle "Colchester Castle").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-11)

**Aswad** are a British [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae "Reggae") group, noted for adding strong [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B") and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") influences to the reggae sound.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-1) They have been performing since the mid-1970s, and have released 21 albums. Their [UK hit singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") include the [number one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chart-topper "Chart-topper") "[Don't Turn Around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Turn_Around "Don't Turn Around")" (1988) and "[Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shine_(Aswad_song) "Shine (Aswad song)")" (1994). "Aswad" is [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language") for "[black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black "Black")". They are three-time [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nominees.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aswad&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The members of Aswad are UK descendants of immigrants from the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). They attended John Kelly/[Holland Park School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Park_School "Holland Park School"). Aswad was formed in 1975 in the [Ladbroke Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladbroke_Grove "Ladbroke Grove") area of [West London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_London "West London").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-3)

The original members of Aswad were guitarist/vocalist [Brinsley "Chaka B" Forde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brinsley_Forde "Brinsley Forde"), drummer/vocalist [Angus "Drummie Zeb" Gaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummie_Zeb "Drummie Zeb"), lead guitarist/vocalist Donald "Dee" Griffiths, bassist George "Ras" Oban, and keyboardist Courtney "Khaki" Hemmings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) Aswad were the backing band of [Burning Spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_Spear "Burning Spear")'s 1977 _[Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_(Burning\_Spear\_album) "Live (Burning Spear album)")_ album, recorded at the [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre") in London. Other contributors included [Vin Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vin_Gordon "Vin Gordon"), and [Karl Pitterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Pitterson "Karl Pitterson").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Larkin-5)

Initially, the band produced music in the [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") vein, with members contributing songs individually and with Forde acting as the band's principal songwriter. The band's dynamic soon began to change however. Shortly after the release of their self-titled debut album in 1976, Hemmings left and was replaced by Tony "Gad" Robinson (the only time in the band's history where a departing member would be officially replaced by an incoming musician). The band then released their second studio effort, _Hulet_, in 1978, before George Oban ( who later played with [Burning Spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_Spear "Burning Spear") and [African Headcharge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Headcharge "African Headcharge") ) departed the band in 1979, with Robinson taking over the position of bassist as well as continuing his role as keyboardist. The following year saw Griffiths depart, leaving Forde as the band's sole guitarist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) During this early period in the band's history they were distinctly different from Jamaican reggae acts, in that they wrote songs that dealt with the issues surrounding the experiences of black youths growing-up in the UK;[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-Moskowitz-4) such as "Three Babylon" and "It's Not Our Wish","Natural Progression", "Ghetto in the Sky". and the powerful [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")-influenced [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental "Instrumental") "Warrior Charge", which is still much played by [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") sound systems worldwide. The band continued making [roots reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_reggae "Roots reggae") and dub music, and in 1985, released _[Jah Shaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jah\_Shaka "Jah Shaka") Meets Aswad in [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis\_Ababa "Addis Ababa") Studio._

Once the band's line-up had stabilised into the trio of Forde, Gaye, and Robinson, Aswad followed a more commercial reggae style, gaining a wider audience with the _New Chapter_ album (1981). They then followed this with the Michael Reuben Campbell-produced _[A New Chapter of Dub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_New\_Chapter\_of\_Dub "A New Chapter of Dub")_ LP which was a dub of the entire _New Chapter_ album. Clifton "Bigga" Morrison of [Prince Far I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Far_I "Prince Far I")'s band, The Arabs, played bass on some of the tracks. _Not Satisfied_ was a London roots-reggae album released in 1982. In August 1983, Aswad played live at [Meanwhile Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meanwhile_Gardens "Meanwhile Gardens") on the Sunday of the [Notting Hill Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_Carnival "Notting Hill Carnival"); the resulting live album _Live and Direct_ is a faithful record of that event, where they played a live dub set. "Love Fire" gained wide recognition when it was used as the [backing rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riddim "Riddim") for [Dennis Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Brown "Dennis Brown")'s "Promised Land".

Among Aswad's catalogue of [hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_single "Hit single") is "[Don't Turn Around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Turn_Around "Don't Turn Around")", a UK No. 1 hit in 1988,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-6) originally recorded by [Tina Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Turner "Tina Turner") as a [B-side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-side_and_B-side "A-side and B-side") to her "[Typical Male](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typical_Male "Typical Male")" single. They followed this up with UK No. 11 hit "Give a Little Love",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-6) and a reggae-flavoured rendition of "[Best of My Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_of_My_Love_(Eagles_song) "Best of My Love (Eagles song)")", first popularised and written by [The Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eagles "The Eagles"). In 1989, they contributed the single "Set Them Free" to the [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace")_Rainbow Warriors_ album. In the same year, they performed together with [Cliff Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliff_Richard "Cliff Richard") the song "Share a Dream", recorded the previous year, at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium") as part of The Event (16 and 17 June 1989). Their next single, "[Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shine_(Aswad_song) "Shine (Aswad song)")", was released in 1994 and was a big hit in much of Europe. Another track was the upbeat 1998 remake of [The Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Police "The Police")'s "[Invisible Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invisible_Sun "Invisible Sun")", performed with [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)").

The band also hold the distinction of having played with each one of the ex-[Wailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wailers_(1963-1974_band) "The Wailers (1963-1974 band)").

The band has toured extensively, playing in diverse locations from London's [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") and [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay")'s [Reggae Sunsplash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae_Sunsplash "Reggae Sunsplash"), to gigs in West Africa, [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") and Japan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-7)

Aswad underwent their first line-up change in sixteen years in 1996, when Forde departed the band for spiritual reasons, leaving Gaye as the only founding member. Once again, the remaining members opted not to seek to recruit a replacement musician, and thus Aswad became a duo of Gaye and Robinson. With the exception of a brief reunion with Forde in 2009 for the Island record label's 50th-anniversary celebrations,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-8) the band's line-up remained the same until Angus Gaye’s death on 2 September 2022, aged 62.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-9)

Aswad released their final studio album to date in 2009, with _City Lock_. They released the singles "What Is Love?" and "Do That Thing" in the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-10)

Aswad toured the UK in Spring 2025, including playing at the [Lambeth Country Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Country_Show "Lambeth Country Show"), at [Butlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butlins "Butlins") resorts, [Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth "Bournemouth")'s Reggae Weekender, and with [Ali Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Campbell "Ali Campbell")'s [UB40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UB40 "UB40") at [Colchester Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester_Castle "Colchester Castle").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswad#cite_note-11)
